items.title: 19.1.2 Chemical Composition and Organization of Chromosome

source_refs.note: Topic 19.1.2 with the Tidbit (PDF 117-118); Figures 19.3 and 19.4 are replaced by the original diagram.

blocks.text: A chromosome is made up of 40% DNA and 60% proteins (histones). Both chromatids have identical DNA molecules. The DNA in an average human chromosome is about 5 cm long and consists of about 140 million nucleotides. DNA is a negatively charged due to the presence of phosphate groups. It has strong affinity to histone proteins, which are positively charged due to the abundance of basic amino acids such as arginine and lysine. The following are the levels of the organization of chromosomes.

After replication, approximately every 146 nucleotides of DNA (2 nm thick) wrap twice around a histone octamer (set of 8 histone molecules i.e., two copies each of the histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4). So, aggregations called nucleosomes are formed. Nucleosomes are connected by about 80 nucleotide long linker DNA. The fifth type of histone i.e., H1 called linker histone is present at the base of the nucleosome near the DNA entry and exit points. It helps in the winding of the chain of nucleosomes. All nucleosomes (without linker histone) resemble beads on a string called nucleosome string (11 nm thick).

blocks.alt: Top: a histone octamer drawn as a disc in two layers, its top divided into four coloured histones H2B, H3, H4 and H2A. Plus a wavy DNA strand of about 146 nucleotides. A green arrow leads to a nucleosome string: DNA wound round three octamers like beads on a string, with the histone H1 at the base of a nucleosome.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.3: Nucleosome string (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.3).
blocks.long_description: Labels: H2B, H3, H4, H2A, Histone octamer, DNA (about 146 nucleotides), Nucleosome, H1, Nucleosome string.

blocks.alt: One continuous drawing from top to bottom: the DNA double helix (2 nm); the DNA wound round red histone octamers to make nucleosomes joined by linker DNA, with a yellow linker histone on each (11 nm); the nucleosomes packed into a chromatin fibre (30 nm); the fibre folded into loops, the supercoil (300 nm); the loops coiled tightly into condensed chromatin (700 nm); and finally the duplicated chromosome, one chromatid 700 nm wide and both chromatids together 1,400 nm.
blocks.caption: Figure 19.4: Organization of chromosome (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 19.4).
blocks.long_description: Labels: DNA, 2 nm, Histone octamer, Nucleosome, Linker DNA, Linker histone, 11 nm, Chromatin fibre, 30 nm, Supercoil, 300 nm, Condensed chromatin, 700 nm, Chromatid, 700 nm, 1,400 nm.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 19.4 labels one chromatid 1,400 nm, while the book's text gives a chromatid as 700 nm. A chromatid is 700 nm; 1,400 nm is the width of the whole chromosome of two chromatids, as drawn above.
In the early stages of cell division, the nucleosome string again coils about its axis. Tightly packed (condensed) nucleosomes make a thicker fibre called chromatin fibre (30 nm).

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: There are two regions in chromatin. The inactive portions of chromatin produce dark bands and are called heterochromatin. Whereas active portions of chromosomes are called euchromatin.
The chromatin fibre folds upon itself to make a supercoil (300 nm thick). The supercoil further coils and condenses and takes the shape of chromatid (700 nm thick).
